title: The Elegant Flirt 4
content:
Lan Wangji didn’t spare Wei Wuxian a glance. Offering a disciplined, minimal nod of greeting, he kept his voice level: “Liberation first, suppression second, elimination third. Begin with their family, touching their heart to satisfy their dying wish and dissolve their lingering obsession. If that fails, suppress it. If the crime is unforgivable and its malice refuses to fade, dig it out by the root, wiping it from existence entirely. When operating in the cultivation world, one must follow this order to the letter. There is no room for error.”

The entire room let out a collective, breathless sigh of relief. Thank the heavens the old man picked Lan Wangji. If it had fallen on any of them, they were bound to mix up an order or bungle a term. Lan Qiren nodded in deep approval. “Not a single word out of place.” He paused, his gaze sweeping sharply across the hall. “Whether cultivating your spiritual path or cultivating your character, this is the exact, unyielding foundation required. If anyone thinks that hunting a few third-rate mountain spirits back home and coasting on hollow fame earns them the right to strut around, acting wildly above the rules, they are cruising for a bitter humiliation sooner rather than later.”

Wei Wuxian’s eyebrow twitched. He stole a look at Lan Wangji’s pristine profile and chuckled quietly to himself: So the old coot is gunning for me after all. Dragging his star pupil into class was just an elaborate excuse to put me in my place.

He raised his hand. “I have a doubt.”

Lan Qiren’s beard bristled. “Speak.”

“Everyone says liberation comes first,” Wei Wuxian drawled, “but in the real world, liberation is practically a fantasy. It’s easy to talk about ‘fulfilling a dying wish to melt away obsession.’ That’s all fine and dandy if the ghost just wants a nice new set of robes. But what happens if its obsession is slaughtering an entire clan down to the dog for bloody revenge? What do you do then?”

Lan Wangji replied without missing a beat: “Thus, prioritize liberation, reinforce with suppression, and eliminate only when necessary.”

Wei Wuxian offered a lazy grin. “Such a waste of good material.” He leaned against his desk, pausing for effect before adding, “It’s not like I didn’t know the textbook answer. I was just weighing a fourth option.”

Lan Qiren frowned severely. “There is no fourth option.”

“Consider the executioner,” Wei Wuxian argued smoothly. “He died a violent death, so turning into a vicious fierce corpse is practically guaranteed. But in life, he beheaded well over a hundred men. Why not simply dig up those hundred graves, whip their resentment into a frenzy, bind their hundred severed heads together, and set them loose to tear that executioner apart…?”

Lan Wangji finally turned his head to look at him, his brow furrowing as a look of icy, unmasked distaste settled across his features. Up at the lectern, Lan Qiren’s goatee was practically vibrating with rage.

“Insolent fool!” he barked, the sudden roar shocking the Orchid Room into dead silence.

Lan Qiren slammed his hands onto the desk and surged to his feet. “Subduing demons, pacifying monsters, and purging evil spirits exists solely for the purpose of guiding souls toward peace! You don't spare a single thought for righteous liberation; instead, you plot to stoke malice and whip up dark energy?! You put the cart before the horse! You trample over basic human decency!”

Wei Wuxian held his ground, entirely unfazed. “Look, some things simply can’t be purified anyway, so why not put them to work? Even Yu the Great knew that when managing a flood, damming the water is a fool's gamble, while carving channels to redirect the flow is true genius. Suppression is just putting up a dam—isn't that inherently the worst possible move…?”

Lan Qiren hurled a heavy parchment book straight at his face. Wei Wuxian tilted his head, letting the projectile whistle harmlessly past his ear, and kept spinning his heresy without dropping a beat. “Spiritual energy is energy; resentful energy is energy too. Spiritual energy is cultivated in the core, capable of splitting mountains and parting oceans for mortal use. Why shouldn’t resentful energy be harnessed the exact same way?”

Whack! A second volume went flying toward his head. Lan Qiren’s voice turned deadly sharp: “Then answer me this! How do you guarantee this dark energy serves you instead of turning around and butchering innocent lives?!”

Dodging the flying scripture, Wei Wuxian shot back, “Haven’t figured that part out yet!”

Lan Qiren’s face flushed an apoplectic crimson. “If you ever do, the cultivation world won't suffer your existence for a single day! Get the hell out!”

Music to my ears. Wei Wuxian didn’t wait to be told twice; he rolled out of the room before the old man could wind up for a third toss.

He spent the rest of the afternoon loafing around the Cloud Recesses, picking wild mountain blooms and idling away the hours. By the time lectures finally wrapped, the other boys had to scour the grounds before finally tracking him down perched atop a soaring tiled wall. Wei Wuxian was lounging comfortably on the dark roof ridge, a long stem of wild orchid dangling from his lips. Resting his chin in his hand with one knee pulled up to his chest, his other leg hung lazily off the eaves, swinging back and forth in the breeze.

The crowd below clustered around, pointing up at him. “Brother Wei! Man, respect! When he told you to scram, you actually bailed on the spot! Hahaha...”

“You should’ve seen his face! It took him forever to realize you actually walked out. He went completely purple!”

Wei Wuxian chewed on the stem, calling down into the courtyard, “I answered his questions, and I left when I was told to leave. What more does the guy want from me?”

Nie Huaisang fanned himself, clicking his tongue. “Seriously though, why does the old man have such a massive bone to pick with you? He singled you out just to drag you through the mud!”

Jiang Cheng scoffed, crossing his arms. “He brought it on himself. Who on earth spews that kind of unhinged garbage in class? Babbling about that nonsense in the privacy of your own bedroom is one thing, but pitching it directly to Lan Qiren’s face? Pure suicidal tendencies.”

“Come on, he was going to hate me regardless of what came out of my mouth,” Wei Wuxian dismissed breezily. “I might as well speak my mind and get some kicks out of it. It’s not like I swore at him—I was just being honest.”

Nie Huaisang paused, his eyes widening with a faint, dreamy fascination. “Though to be honest, what Brother Wei said actually sounded pretty incredible. Spiritual energy demands endless sweat and grinding just to form a Golden Core. With my garbage aptitude—born like my brain was chewed by wild dogs in the womb—heaven only knows how many decades I'll have to waste. But resentful energy already belongs to those terrifying ghosts! If you could just scoop it up and weaponize it right out of the box, how amazing would that be?”

A Golden Core was a condensed sphere of spiritual essence formed inside a cultivator once they crossed a critical threshold, serving as the engine to generate, circulate, and store spiritual energy. Once that core formed, a cultivator’s growth skyrocketed, allowing them to scale the higher peaks of the path. Without it, you were practically a scrub. For a scion of a prominent family to form their core late in life was considered a deeply humiliating failure, yet Nie Huaisang admitted it with zero shame.

Wei Wuxian barked a laugh. “Right?! Free fuel—it’s practically a crime not to use it!”

Jiang Cheng’s eyes narrowed into slits. “Enough. You can joke about it, but don't you dare even think about walking down that twisted ditch.”

Wei Wuxian grinned. “Why would I trade a sunlit highway for a rickety single-plank bridge over an open sewer? If that bridge were so easy to cross, someone would’ve conquered it centuries ago. Relax, he tossed out a hypothetical, so I threw back a theory. Anyway, you guys in or what? We still have time before curfew—come shoot wild pheasants with me!”

“Shoot wild pheasants? Where the hell are you going to find wild pheasants in these pristine mountains?!” Jiang Cheng barked. “Go copy the Righteousness Chapter, you idiot. Lan Qiren told me to pass along your punishment: copy the Righteousness Chapter of the Gusu Rules of Discipline three full times, just so you can learn what natural law and basic morality actually mean!”

The Rules of Discipline was the Lan Clan’s sacred household code. Their rules were absurdly verbose, and after Lan Qiren’s relentless revisions over the decades, they had bloated into a massive, doorstopper encyclopedia. The Righteousness Chapter and the Etiquette Chapter alone made up four-fifths of the entire manuscript.

Wei Wuxian spat the grass stem out, knocking the dust off his boots. “Three times?! Copying that monstrosity once is enough to make me ascend to heaven! I’m not a Lan, and I sure as hell don’t plan on marrying into their family—why am I copying their family handbook? Not happening.”

Nie Huaisang raised his hand in a flash. “I’ll copy it for you! I’ll do it!”

Wei Wuxian squinted down at him. “Unsolicited kindness always hides a sneaky motive. Spill it: what do you want from me?”

Nie Huaisang winced. “Well, Brother Wei, the old man has this terrible habit. He—”

The boy snapped his mouth shut mid-sentence, cleared his throat, and instantly snapped his folding fan open, shrinking into the background. Smelling trouble, Wei Wuxian glanced sideways. Sure enough, standing beneath the dappled canopy of an ancient oak was Lan Wangji, Bichen resting across his back, watching them from a distance. He stood straight as a jade pillar against the sun and shadow, but his stare was as cold as a frozen cavern; catching that glare was enough to make your blood run icy. Realizing their hollering across the roofs had broken the peace and reeled in the hall monitor, the group instinctively clamped their mouths shut.

Wei Wuxian, however, hopped down from the wall with a grin, jogging toward him. “Brother Wangji!”

Lan Wangji turned on his heel and walked away.

Wei Wuxian picked up his pace, calling out cheerfully, “Brother Wangji, hey! Wait up!”

A flutter of white robes flashed past the cedar trunks, vanishing into thin air within a heartbeat. The boy clearly had zero interest in trading words. Left eating a trail of cold dust, Wei Wuxian wandered back to the group, pouting with dramatic betrayal. “He completely ignored me.”

“Well, yeah,” Nie Huaisang muttered. “Seems he truly despises you, Brother Wei. Lan Wangji is usually… well, actually, he’s never this overtly rude to anyone.”

Wei Wuxian tilted his head. “He hates me already? And here I was, honestly trying to apologize to the guy.”

Jiang Cheng sneered, “Apologizing now? Too late! He thinks just like his uncle—convinced you’re crooked to the bone, rotten inside and out. He won’t waste breath on you.”

Wei Wuxian waved it off with an unbothered smirk. “Whatever, let him ignore me. Does being pretty give him the right to act like a snob?” He paused, picturing that face again, and thought: Well, okay, he really is absurdly pretty. Comforted by the thought, any urge to stay annoyed evaporated completely.

Three days later, Wei Wuxian finally discovered what Lan Qiren’s "terrible habit" was.

The old man’s lectures were already dreadfully tedious, but to make matters worse, he insisted on testing every single syllable via closed-book dictation: shifts in clan territories across generations, boundary realignments, famous quotes from celebrated masters, intricate clan genealogies…

Listening to the lectures felt like deciphering celestial gibberish; sitting down to write the exams was straight-up penal labor.

Nie Huaisang had already forged two copies of the Righteousness Chapter for Wei Wuxian, but as the exam drew near, he fell to his knees in tears. “Brother Wei, I’m begging you! This is my third year getting sent back to Gusu! If I don't pull at least an average grade this time, my big brother will break my legs for real! What kind of exam expects us to memorize main branches versus side branches of distant clans?! We’re young masters—half of us can barely figure out our own second cousins twice-removed without making a mess of our titles, so who the hell has the extra brain space to memorize other people’s family trees?!”

The inevitable consequence of cheat sheets flying through the air like autumn leaves was Lan Wangji materializing out of nowhere midway through the exam, catching the ringleaders red-handed.

Lan Qiren went into an absolute, howling fury, firing off urgent letters of complaint to every major sect leader. The rage burned a hole in the elder’s gut: originally, while these aristocratic brats had been restless, nobody had dared step out of line, managing to keep their rear ends glued to their cushions. But the second Wei Ying set foot on this mountain, he’d coaxed every coward into mischief! Midnight prowling, black-market drinking—crooked habits were spreading like weeds! This Wei Ying was precisely the human catastrophe he’d anticipated: a walking, breathing public menace!

Jiang Fengmian’s written reply arrived promptly: A-Ying has always been lively. We trouble Master Lan to discipline him as you see fit.

And so, Wei Wuxian was slammed with another punishment.

At first, he didn't care in the slightest. Copying texts was nothing; he never lacked eager volunteers willing to take the brush for him. But this time, Nie Huaisang wrung his hands miserably. “Brother Wei, I can't save you this time. You’re on your own.”

Wei Wuxian frowned. “Why?”

“The old… Master Lan gave specific orders. This time, you have to copy both the Righteousness Chapter and the Etiquette Chapter together.”

The Etiquette Chapter was the most bloated, grueling monstrosity of the twelve chapters in the Lan code. Packed with obscure archaic quotes and endless strokes, writing it once was enough to kill your will to live; writing it ten times would see you ascending straight to Nirvana.

Nie Huaisang added in a whisper, “And he said that during your detention, nobody is allowed to hang around you, and nobody is permitted to write a single stroke on your behalf.”

Wei Wuxian tilted his head. “How would he even know if someone helped me? It’s not like he’s going to plant a guard to breathe down my neck while I write.”

Jiang Cheng crossed his arms. “That is precisely what he’s doing.”

Wei Wuxian blinked. “...Say that again?”

“You are confined to the premises every single day,” Jiang Cheng said, relishing the misery. “You're to sit in the Lan Clan's Library Pavilion, copying the scriptures while facing the wall to reflect on your crimes for an entire month. And of course there’s a guard. As for who it is, do I really need to spell it out for you?”

Inside the Library Pavilion.

A single woven rush mat, a low wooden desk. Two candleholders, two boys.

At one end of the mat sat a figure in pristine, unyielding stillness. At the other end, Wei Wuxian had already slogged through more than ten pages of the Etiquette Chapter. His head was swimming, his brain felt thoroughly scrambled, and boredom was clawing at his skull. Tossing his brush aside to catch his breath, his eyes drifted toward the boy across from him.

Back in Yunmeng, plenty of girls had gushed over how lucky he was to share a classroom with Lan Wangji, endlessly gossiping about the Lan Clan churning out generations of heartthrobs and how this era’s Twin Jades were peerless beauties. Wei Wuxian hadn't had the time to study the guy's face up close before, but inspecting him now, his thoughts began to wander: He really is ridiculously good-looking. The features, the posture—you can’t find a single flaw to nitpick. Though I really wish those squealing maidens could see him in person; if you walk around all day glaring at everyone like someone murdered your family, no amount of pretty bone structure can save your personality.

Lan Wangji was busy re-transcribing ancient, fragile texts from the library’s private archives—volumes too sacred and delicate for outsiders’ eyes. His brush moved with steady, measured strokes, carving characters that stood sharp, elegant, and upright with internal strength.

Wei Wuxian couldn't help letting out an honest, unfiltered compliment: “Incredible calligraphy! Absolute top tier.”

Lan Wangji didn't twitch a muscle.

Going mute for this long was practically torture for Wei Wuxian. Feeling suffocated, he grumbled internally: This guy is as lively as a tombstone. Forcing me to sit across from him for hours a day, for an entire month—he might as well just put a sword through my chest!

At the thought, he couldn't resist leaning his upper body slightly forward across the desk.
